segments.title: Uncrewed encounters expose gaps in maritime law
segments.body: An encounter between a Russian frigate's small uncrewed aircraft and a Danish uncrewed surface vessel raises a basic legal problem: neither side places a crew directly at risk. Much of international maritime law developed around danger to human life, so it does not give an easy answer about when this kind of buzzing becomes an unlawful act. The political context also changes the risk calculation, since a provocative approach during high tension may receive a more restrained response than the same surprise during a quiet period. Repeated encounters will help shape practice, but the rules remain unsettled.

evidence.note: The question and answer discuss uncrewed encounters, harm to people, maritime law, and escalation risk.

segments.question: How should maritime law treat an uncrewed aircraft buzzing an uncrewed surface vessel?
segments.answerShort: Existing rules focus heavily on risks to people, leaving uncertain thresholds for harassment and force when both assets are uncrewed.

segments.title: A 1938 speed refit for Nelson and Rodney
segments.body: A comprehensive refit could replace the machinery and, if the hull were lengthened, improve the ships' reliable all-weather speed by several knots. The estimate is about 25 or 26 knots in place of the declared 23-knot safe maximum. That extra speed matters because Rodney historically came close to catching Gneisenau. A faster Nelson-class battleship could force a battle in which its nine 16-inch guns and heavy protection confronted Gneisenau's nine 11-inch guns.

evidence.note: The answer estimates a 25 to 26 knot refit and applies it to a possible Rodney and Gneisenau engagement.

segments.question: What could a full 1938 refit do for Nelson and Rodney's speed and wartime value?
segments.answerShort: Modern boilers and a lengthened hull might lift their dependable speed to roughly 25 or 26 knots, making German escape much harder.

segments.title: Mers-el-Kebir as a communications failure
segments.body: The French admiral had narrow instructions and little freedom to improvise, while communication between the French government, its officers, and Britain had already failed badly. Rank also mattered because the British negotiator spoke French but was not senior enough to satisfy the admiral receiving him. British demands included moving the fleet to distant French territory, where it could remain French while staying beyond easy German control. One counterfactual places it in French Indochina, where a later Japanese attack could bring the war in the Far East forward and complicate Germany's relationship with both France and Japan. Joining the Free French was Britain's preferred outcome, and removing the ships from the combat area came next. With the whole French Navy joining the Allies, the added force is expected to bring the Mediterranean and North African campaigns to an early end. The central British fear was that the French government could order crews ashore and hand their ships to Germany, even if the sailors had no intention of fighting Britain. Sinking the ships was the worst option on the British list, chosen because assurances from a government that had left the war no longer seemed sufficient protection against a German seizure.

evidence.note: The answer traces French orders, negotiator rank, British options, German seizure fears, and the hierarchy of preferred outcomes.

segments.question: Was the British attack at Mers-el-Kebir mainly the result of French pride and incompetence?
segments.answerShort: The crisis grew from poor orders, broken communication, rank sensitivities, and British fear that the French fleet might be handed to Germany.

segments.title: Scottish independence, Faslane, and naval shipbuilding
segments.body: A long Faslane lease is possible, although it is considered unlikely. Support for the Scottish National Party does not translate consistently into support for independence; many voters appear to want stronger representation of Scottish interests within the existing union. Naval construction would become part of the settlement because current contracts require work in British territory. Yards now in Scotland could lose future orders if they were outside that territory, while other parts of the United Kingdom could compete for the work. Basing, industrial policy, and electoral politics would therefore be tied together in any serious negotiation.

evidence.note: The answer covers a possible Faslane lease, Scottish voting behavior, and the territorial requirements attached to shipbuilding contracts.

segments.question: Would Scottish independence lead to a long lease of Faslane similar to Hong Kong?
segments.answerShort: A lease is possible but judged unlikely, and independence would also reopen where British warship contracts and yards must be located.

segments.title: Preferred unbuilt battleships and battlecruisers
segments.body: G3 and K2 are among the first choices, followed by F3 as a post-World War I successor to HMS Tiger. Even one F3 alongside Nelson and Rodney could change Britain's supply of fast capital ships, particularly when older battlecruisers needed maintenance. N3 appeals because its protection was intended to resist 18-inch guns while its own heavy battery threatened an opponent. Another panellist later chooses Montana. These are personal preferences for unbuilt designs, with operational availability and protection explaining some of their appeal.

evidence.note: The panel chooses G3, K2, F3, and N3, explaining F3's value as a fast-ship alternative during maintenance and N3's intended protection.
A panellist adds Montana to the preferred unbuilt ships.

segments.question: Which planned but unbuilt battleship or battlecruiser would each panellist choose to see completed?
segments.answerShort: The choices include G3, K2, F3, N3, and Montana, with different preferences for fast battlecruisers and heavily protected battleships.

segments.title: How completed N3s could enlarge Yamato
segments.body: The counterfactual assumes that British N3 construction allows further capital-ship development before an arms agreement, perhaps delaying the Washington settlement until about 1926. Japanese 18-inch ships could then help establish a treaty ceiling around 50,000 tons and 18-inch guns. Yamato's stated aim of engaging two treaty battleships would become a much larger design problem. Twelve 21-inch guns are suggested as one possible response. Such a ship would demand new infrastructure, with the panel considering either extending a dry dock into the mountain behind it or reclaiming part of a bay.

evidence.note: A follow-up asks how one or two N3s would affect Yamato. The response proposes a later treaty, larger gun and displacement limits, a twelve-gun 21-inch battery, and major dock construction.

segments.question: How would one or two completed N3 battleships change the later Yamato class?
segments.answerShort: Later treaty limits could rise to 18-inch guns and about 50,000 tons, pushing a Yamato intended to defeat two treaty battleships toward twelve 21-inch guns and new dock facilities.

segments.title: Japan's big ships as a deterrent
segments.body: The big-ship, big-gun approach is interpreted as a deterrence policy as well as a way to fight a battle. If Japan could crew only a limited number of ships, enlarging each hull offered a way to increase the apparent strength of that force. Building ships comparable to everyone else's would let a richer opponent answer by adding one more. A much larger individual ship would force that opponent to consider a more difficult and expensive response. The argument concerns the deterrent effect of the fleet's appearance and capabilities.

evidence.note: The discussion distinguishes Japanese big-ship deterrence from battlefield usefulness and explains the constraint imposed by the number of ships that could be crewed.

segments.summary: An oversized battleship could deter opponents by making each Japanese hull harder to match when crew numbers limited the size of the fleet.

segments.title: Choosing a Royal Navy ballistic missile interceptor
segments.body: Both interceptors remain credible options because future British ships can carry strategic-length Mark 41 and Sylver cells. SM-3 earns confidence from its test record and established performance. Aquila has a stronger logistics case because it belongs with systems Britain already operates and is being designed for both launcher families. The preference therefore divides between affection for SM-3 and the practical advantages of a European weapon with common support arrangements.

evidence.note: The answer compares SM-3 experience with Aquila logistics and launcher compatibility.

segments.question: Should the Royal Navy adopt SM-3 or the MBDA Aquila family for ballistic missile defence?
segments.answerShort: SM-3 has proven appeal, while Aquila better fits the missile families and logistics already used by Britain.

segments.title: Foreign frigate construction for the US Navy
segments.body: Purchasing a foreign design for construction in American yards leaves many suppliers in contention. Buying complete ships overseas narrows the field because few countries have available yard capacity, leaving Japan and South Korea as the main options. Japanese sales experience is judged stronger at present, making the Mogami family a plausible result even though South Korea also offers capable designs. The outcome depends as much on available production capacity as on the quality of the design.

evidence.note: The answer separates foreign design purchase from overseas construction and identifies Japanese and South Korean capacity.

segments.question: What might follow from a US move toward the Finnish model of foreign frigate construction?
segments.answerShort: Buying a design for US construction leaves many choices, while overseas construction is likely limited to Japanese or South Korean yards with spare capacity.

segments.title: Why the Royal Navy does not need a naval GCAP
segments.body: A carrier-capable GCAP would create another expensive variant for a requirement already met by F-35B. Repeating the three-version structure of the F-35 program would require a compelling operational need. A naval Gripen able to use a ski-jump carrier may offer a cheaper crewed complement. That option also matters because uncrewed aircraft may struggle in electronically hostile conditions where their links and control systems cannot be trusted.

evidence.note: The answer rejects an additional GCAP variant, points to F-35B, and discusses Gripen and uncrewed-aircraft limitations.

segments.question: Should the Royal Navy have its own carrier-capable GCAP variant?
segments.answerShort: The cost of a separate carrier variant is hard to justify while F-35B exists, and a naval Gripen may offer a cheaper crewed alternative to uncrewed aircraft.

segments.title: How other powers might answer the Zepang super battleship
segments.body: A ship of this scale would probably prevent the Washington treaty system from emerging in its familiar form. Other navies could delay laying down a direct rival until Japan proved the project workable, since the attempt might overwhelm Japanese heavy industry. Britain and the United States would still have reason to start the required infrastructure: the estimate allows three to five years for the docks and another three to five for a ship. If Zepang failed, those yards could serve other large construction. If it entered service after five years while rivals had delayed every response, they could face another five years before completing an answer. Political pressure could then force them to build an equally impractical vessel despite its poor fit with their strategy.

evidence.note: The answer discusses treaty effects, industrial risk, dock construction, and political pressure to respond.

segments.question: How would other powers react if Japan attempted a 500,000-ton Zepang battleship?
segments.answerShort: They might wait to see whether Japan could finish it, while beginning the docks and yards needed to answer it if the project succeeded.

segments.title: Why thirty useful years still justify a warship
segments.body: The fact that a later weapon may supersede a ship does not erase the value delivered before that change. Thirty years from 1914 reaches 1944, covering almost all of both world wars. Aircraft and submarines developed throughout that period, yet battleships remained necessary for diplomacy, fleet operations, and wartime missions for much of it. Before snorkels, submarines spent most of their time on the surface under diesel power and were closer to torpedo boats that could occasionally submerge. Naval aviation and submarines reached something closer to equal standing with battleships only near the end of that span. Refusing a needed capability because a future system may eventually replace it can leave a navy exposed for an entire generation.

evidence.note: The discussion uses 1914 to 1944 to explain why eventual obsolescence does not remove decades of operational value.
The speakers describe pre-snorkel submarines as surface-running torpedo boats that submerged only occasionally.

segments.summary: A reply to claims that future bombers would make a giant battleship pointless explains how much military and diplomatic value can fit into thirty years.

segments.title: An enlarged Type 45 after the Falklands War
segments.body: The Canadian Power alternate history gives its Type 45 a 144-cell missile battery: groups of 64 and 48 Sylver A70 cells plus 32 Mark 48 cells. The 10,720-ton hull also carries twin 155 mm guns, two quadruple Harpoon launchers, close-range guns, and two triple 324 mm torpedo-tube mountings. The scenario links this enlarged design to the loss of two Type 42 destroyers and two Type 21 frigates in the Falklands. Those losses could create a political demand that no future ship lack layered protection. The response treats the imagined fit as an excessive expression of that demand, joking that even its guns look restrained beside the rest of the armament.

evidence.note: The question specifies the Canadian Power scenario's 144 cells, divided into 64 and 48 Sylver A70 cells and 32 Mark 48 cells, twin 155 mm guns, Harpoons, close-range weapons, torpedo tubes, displacement, and losses. The answer links the design to a reaction against layered-defence failure.

segments.question: How could the loss of two Type 42 destroyers and two Type 21 frigates in the Falklands lead to the heavily armed Type 45 in the Canadian Power alternate history?
segments.answerShort: The losses could trigger a determination to prevent another gap in layered defence, although the imagined design still overinvests in weapons.

segments.title: How many carriers the Regia Marina needed
segments.body: A 15,000-ton carrier could provide fighters and reconnaissance, but it would offer little strike depth. A more capable ship for the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean would resemble other 27,000-ton prewar carriers. The proposed force needs two ships for the Mediterranean and one or preferably two available for the ocean, with additional hulls required for maintenance and rotation. That produces an estimate of six to eight carriers and roughly 208,000 tons of carrier construction. A ceiling closer to 270,000 tons would make the deployment pattern easier to sustain.

evidence.note: The answer estimates carrier size and numbers for Mediterranean and Indian Ocean deployments, including the final 270,000-ton alternative.

segments.question: How many prewar carriers, and of what size, would the Regia Marina need?
segments.answerShort: Six to eight carriers of about 27,000 tons would support strike operations in the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean, while smaller ships could cover only fighters and reconnaissance.

segments.title: A rebuilt Hood changes the hunt for Bismarck
segments.body: Removing Hood from service could keep King George V and Prince of Wales together instead of splitting them. Renown and Ark Royal might be recalled, with Victorious adding another carrier air group. Tovey could command the battleships and carriers while Somerville handled Renown and the cruisers. Bismarck would then face repeated air strikes and several heavy ships from different directions, leaving no safe choice of target. Prinz Eugen's best plausible escape would still involve dealing with Renown and two County-class cruisers.

evidence.note: The answer assembles an alternate force of King George V, Prince of Wales, Renown, Ark Royal, Victorious, and cruisers against Bismarck.

segments.question: What if turbine damage forced Hood into a major rebuild before the Denmark Strait battle?
segments.answerShort: Hood would miss the battle, while a much larger force built around two King George V battleships, Renown, Ark Royal, Victorious, and cruisers could converge on Bismarck.

segments.title: Possible radar fits for the future CCV
segments.body: A near-term sensor decision is considered unlikely because the funding discussed would support little beyond a research team. Firmer choices are expected after the next general election, identified here as 2029, although the available technology and requirements could change before then. SAMPSON remains one option alongside a full Aegis system and larger Australian or Japanese solid-state arrays. The ship might combine a long-range search radar with fixed arrays for tracking and engagement, or use one integrated system for both jobs. A firm prediction also depends on the hull selected. Growing discussion of an Arrowhead 160, part of a family reportedly extending from about 100 to 180 metres, therefore matters to the radar question.

evidence.note: The answer compares SAMPSON, Aegis, Australian, Japanese, and mixed radar arrangements while stressing that the hull remains undecided. The CCV expansion is checked against the Ministry of Defence's 9 July 2026 answer: https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-questions/detail/2026-06-25/13185. SAMPSON spelling follows the Royal Navy's Daring-class equipment page: https://www.royalnavy.mod.uk/equipment/ships/daring-class.
The follow-up explains the Arrowhead size family and current interest in the 160-metre version.

segments.question: What radar and sensor fit might the future Common Combat Vessel (CCV) receive?
segments.answerShort: SAMPSON, Aegis-related arrays, Australian and Japanese systems, or a mixed long-range and fixed-array fit remain possible until the hull is chosen.

segments.title: Ten-gun Queen Elizabeths at 28 knots
segments.body: A ten-gun battery and 28-knot speed would push the class beyond the historical super-dreadnought standard. The ships could keep pace with many foreign battlecruisers while retaining battleship protection and firepower. Britain would gain a fast battle line instead of having to separate speed from heavy combat power. Other navies would have to answer a class that combined qualities they had expected to face in different ship types.

evidence.note: The answer describes the ships as fast battleships able to match battlecruiser speeds and keep the battle line together.

segments.question: How would ten 15-inch guns and a speed of 28 knots change the Queen Elizabeth class?
segments.answerShort: They would become true fast battleships, able to match many battlecruisers while keeping a heavily armed battle line together.

segments.title: The Vanguard and Le Triomphant collision
segments.body: USS Redfish's return with a cracked pressure hull, damaged steering, and destroyed sonar prompts a comparison with HMS Vanguard and Le Triomphant. Their collision in the Atlantic is offered as a modern example, although public information is limited and the severity of the damage is inferred from lengthy dry-dock repairs. The boats' quietness is suggested as the reason neither detected the other. The accident supports an argument for a fifth SSBN in each fleet because losing one boat to repairs places pressure on a four-boat force. Broad separation of patrol areas is proposed as a way to reduce collision risk without disclosing exact positions.

evidence.note: The answer uses the Vanguard and Le Triomphant collision to discuss damage, quieting, deconfliction, and fleet resilience.

segments.question: Have submarines survived damage comparable to USS Redfish's wartime return?
segments.answerShort: HMS Vanguard and Le Triomphant are suggested as modern examples. Their lengthy repairs imply serious damage, although public details remain limited.

segments.title: How many VLS cells the CCV needs
segments.body: The proposed lower bound is 96 vertical-launch cells. Anything smaller is judged inadequate for the future ship's magazine requirements. About 120 cells is the preferred target, while 128 would be particularly welcome. These figures express a desired fit, with the budget and decisions after the next general election still unresolved.

evidence.note: The answer gives 96 cells as a minimum, about 120 as preferred, and 128 as desirable.

segments.question: How many vertical-launch cells should the future CCV carry?
segments.answerShort: The preferred minimum is 96 cells, with about 120 favoured and 128 welcomed if the budget and hull allow it.

segments.title: Modern Alaska hulls in an age of cheap drones
segments.body: Nuclear propulsion is unlikely because reactor production is already constrained, making gas turbines the practical choice. A twin 8-inch mount is not ready, and even a new twin 5-inch turret would require years of engineering, maintenance planning, testing, and procurement. Single guns gained favour when precision and small numbers of costly missiles dominated threat forecasts. A twin mount raises questions about the angle at which its guns converge on a target, but it can offer a higher rate of fire. Cheap drones have reopened the low end of the attack spectrum, where the number of incoming weapons can drive the defensive requirement. Electronic warfare can defeat the simplest drones, while hardening their controls increases their cost. Fibre-optic control is possible in some settings, but hundreds of miles of cable would impose a substantial weight burden on a drone operating at sea. The proposed completion therefore favours gas turbines and existing single 5-inch mounts. No missile-cell count is supplied, while the wider gun discussion asks how to defeat numerous inexpensive attackers economically.

evidence.note: The answer covers propulsion, gun-development time, precision trends, drone mass, and electronic warfare. It does not estimate the VLS capacity requested in the question.

segments.question: Would six unfinished Alaska hulls receive reactors or gas turbines, what guns could they carry, and how many VLS cells would fit?
segments.answerShort: Gas turbines and existing single 5-inch guns are considered more practical than scarce reactors or undeveloped twin mounts. No VLS capacity is estimated.

segments.title: New Mexico with eight 16-inch guns
segments.body: The historical class carried twelve 14-inch guns in four triple turrets. Replacing them with eight 16-inch guns is considered physically plausible. A firm answer requires a closer examination of the barbette dimensions and structural arrangements. As with many major-calibre changes, the decisive obstacle would probably be willingness to pay for the redesign rather than a simple impossibility.

evidence.note: The answer says eight 16-inch guns are plausible but reserves judgment pending barbette details and cost.

segments.question: Could the New Mexico class have carried eight 16-inch guns in 1917?
segments.answerShort: The conversion appears possible in principle, although the barbette dimensions need closer checking and the cost would be substantial.

segments.title: A Canadian large destroyer to complement the River class
segments.body: A 10,000-ton destroyer is proposed as a companion to Canada's River class. The suggested starting point is Japan's next generation of large destroyers. Canada's industrial position forms part of the reason for looking abroad. The recommendation is to investigate what Japan intends to build, without a specific Canadian weapons or sensor fit proposed.

evidence.note: The answer recommends asking Japan about its next large-destroyer generation as a complement to the River class. The preceding class name is unclear in the TXT, and no detailed Canadian equipment list is supplied.

segments.question: What should Canada fit to a 10,000-ton destroyer intended to complement the River class?
segments.answerShort: Canada should study Japan's next generation of large destroyers because their likely role and systems would complement the Rivers.

segments.title: Royal Navy shell supply and explosive fillings in World War I
segments.body: The Royal Navy was affected by wartime shell demand, although its position appears to have been less severe than the Army's shortage. No one could recall evidence that Amatol broadly replaced Lyddite in large naval shells. Destroyer-ammunition trials may have involved alternative fillings, but that point remains tentative. Broad Amatol substitution in naval ammunition is therefore an open research question rather than an established policy.

evidence.note: The panel distinguishes the Navy's shortage from the Army's and is uncertain about Amatol use beyond possible destroyer-shell testing.

segments.question: Did the Royal Navy suffer the same shell shortage as the Army, and did it substitute Amatol for Lyddite?
segments.answerShort: The Navy faced supply pressure, although apparently less severely than the Army, and broad use of Amatol in large shells remains unconfirmed.

segments.title: Gun-fit choices for the Royal Navy's CCV
segments.body: A 57 mm gun paired with 40 mm weapons would continue the Type 31 approach and produce a dense light-air-defence fit. A 5-inch gun with 40 mm mounts would combine heavier naval gunfire with that lighter layer. Pairing the 5-inch gun with 57 mm weapons would make the overall fit heavier still. The likely choice depends on how much the Ministry of Defence is prepared to spend.

evidence.note: The answer compares three main and secondary gun combinations and makes funding the deciding variable.

segments.question: Should the CCV carry a 127 mm gun or a 57 mm gun, and what gun fit is most likely?
segments.answerShort: The final mix will reveal whether the ship follows the Type 31's lighter fit or receives a heavier 5-inch main gun, with cost likely deciding the choice.

segments.title: Why Navy and Army procurement diverged in World War I
segments.body: The Royal Navy routinely ordered spare engines and parts with new aircraft because the same practice was normal for its ships. Army observers sometimes interpreted this better stock position as underhand competition for supplies. The deeper difference lay in procurement and logistics institutions that had survived the Boer War without the reforms applied to fighting units. Those neglected systems then broke down under the demands of World War I. Peacetime purchasing habits can determine wartime resilience.

evidence.note: The discussion contrasts Navy orders for spares with Army procurement and logistics structures that failed under wartime pressure.

segments.summary: Navy habits such as ordering spare engines and parts created wartime resilience that the Army's unreformed procurement system lacked.

segments.title: Beatty's suppression of the Harper and Bacon reports
segments.body: Beatty is described as making the stronger suppression effort against Harper, although Bacon's report proved harder to contain. Harper and Bacon responded by publishing their work as books. An official report might have circulated mainly among civil servants, MPs, and specialist newspaper readers. A commercial book could be serialized, reproduced, and read by a broad interested public. Suppression therefore increased the reports' visibility and made their arguments more difficult to manage.

evidence.note: The answer compares the attempts to suppress the reports and explains how book publication expanded their public reach.

segments.question: How hard did Beatty try to bury the Harper and Bacon reports, and which was harder to suppress?
segments.answerShort: Bacon's report was harder to bury, while Beatty tried harder against Harper; publication as books gave both arguments a much wider audience.

segments.title: Corruption in the Navy of Samuel Pepys
segments.body: The Navy administered in the age of Samuel Pepys offers a much larger historical comparison. At points, corruption was sufficiently embedded that the practical question became whether it still served the institution. Government grants and proceeds from captured ships generated money that supported Admiralty functions and other expenses. Ministers often declined to ask how the Navy achieved this degree of financial independence. This was a system of patronage and opaque finance rather than a single isolated scandal.

evidence.note: The answer uses the Pepys-era Navy to illustrate entrenched corruption, prize income, and limited government scrutiny.

segments.question: Did the Royal Navy have an equivalent to the US Navy's Fat Leonard scandal?
segments.answerShort: The Pepys-era Navy offers a much larger historical comparison, when corruption was often tolerated so long as the institution still produced ships and revenue.

segments.title: Why German and Japanese smaller guns lacked AP shells
segments.body: The suggested explanation follows the expected targets of the guns. Destroyers and other light vessels usually carry little armour, so a dedicated armour-piercing projectile offers limited benefit. High-explosive and anti-aircraft shells address the surface and air targets those weapons were most likely to engage. Developing another shell type would also consume researchers and money that even major states do not possess in unlimited quantities. This is an interpretation of the likely requirement, without a specific procurement decision identified.

evidence.note: The answer ties the absence of AP ammunition to unarmoured targets and finite research resources.

segments.question: Why did German and Japanese 4-inch and 5-inch guns lack armour-piercing or semi-armour-piercing shells?
segments.answerShort: The likely explanation is that expected targets favoured high-explosive and anti-aircraft ammunition, leaving little incentive to fund a separate armour-piercing shell.

segments.title: Favorite warship appearances and the details behind them
segments.body: The choices span different eras and types, with a few design details driving each preference. HMS Tiger was chosen for her dreadnought-era lines. Lexington-class carriers looked cleaner after their 8-inch guns and associated structures were removed, while Enterprise and HMS Bristol offered distinctive modern silhouettes. HMS Warspite's 1942 camouflage and retained casemated 6-inch secondaries distinguished her from the refitted Valiant and Queen Elizabeth. Another speaker chose HMS Liverpool, then praised County-class lines and the ship's camouflage without clearly connecting the two remarks. The answers tie appearance to hull form, alterations, camouflage, and retained armament.

evidence.note: The first choices include HMS Tiger, the Lexington class after removal of its 8-inch guns, Enterprise, and HMS Bristol.
Further choices identify HMS Warspite's 1942 camouflage and casemates, then name HMS Liverpool before praising County-class lines and camouflage.

segments.question: Which ships stood out to the group for their appearance?
segments.answerShort: Selections ranged from HMS Tiger and the de-gunned Lexington class to HMS Warspite and HMS Liverpool, with hull lines, camouflage, and retained details driving the choices.

segments.title: Why Australian Oberons received Mark 48 torpedoes
segments.body: Australia could retain the proven British Oberon design while drawing ammunition from American supply lines. The Mark 48 fit supported operational ties with the United States and simplified access to its logistics network. It also let the Royal Australian Navy straddle two important defence relationships. The result was a British submarine paired with an American torpedo system for practical alliance reasons.

evidence.note: The panel attributes the Mark 48 fit to relations with the United States and access to American logistics.

segments.question: Why were the Royal Australian Navy's Oberon-class submarines fitted for Mark 48 torpedoes instead of British weapons?
segments.answerShort: The arrangement combined a British-built submarine with American weapons supply and logistics, strengthening interoperability with both partners.

segments.title: Prussian naval colours in peace and war
segments.body: Prussian ships did use a peacetime colour scheme. Its differences from the wartime appearance were subtle enough to make identification difficult in surviving material. The scheme changed as the Prussian service developed into the Imperial German Navy. The distinction was real but visually less pronounced than in British or French examples.

evidence.note: The answer confirms a subtle Prussian peacetime scheme and its later evolution into Imperial German colours.

segments.question: Did Prussian warships have a distinct peacetime colour scheme like British and French ships?
segments.answerShort: They had a peacetime scheme, although it was difficult to distinguish from the wartime appearance and evolved into Imperial German practice.

segments.title: How quickly an SSN can increase reactor power
segments.body: An operating naval reactor remains active at reduced power instead of shutting down completely. That persistent operation contributes some noise, which is one reason a nuclear submarine cannot reproduce the battery-only silence of a diesel-electric boat. It also allows an SSN to demand much more power on short notice. Open sources do not provide a reliable exact ramp time, so only a qualitative judgment is possible. For comparison, a panellist tentatively recalls operators taking one to two weeks to restore an 800 MW civilian reactor after a trip. That starting condition follows a fault and the insertion of control rods to suppress the reaction, with operators then proceeding cautiously. It does not establish the time an already operating submarine reactor needs to increase output.

evidence.note: The panel explains reduced-power naval reactor operation and the absence of precise open-source timings. At 1:30:02 to 1:30:47 a panellist tentatively recalls a one-to-two-week restart for an 800 MW civilian unit after a trip, while stressing the operators' slow approach.

segments.question: How long does an SSN reactor take to move from silent crawling to peak output?
segments.answerShort: A running submarine reactor can increase power quickly because it is never fully shut down, although exact timings are not available in open sources.

segments.title: Identifying the mislabeled HMAS Australia model
segments.body: Two major Australian warships carried the name HMAS Australia. The County-class ship was a heavy cruiser, while the 1911 vessel was a battlecruiser. An echelon arrangement for the wing turrets identifies the earlier battlecruiser rather than the County-class cruiser. Since that ship was disposed of after World War I under treaty requirements, a postwar heavy-cruiser classification would be incorrect. The display appears to have confused the two namesakes.

evidence.note: The discussion uses the echelon turret layout to identify the battlecruiser and distinguish it from the County-class heavy cruiser.

segments.question: Why did a Sydney museum label an echelon-turret HMAS Australia model as a heavy cruiser?
segments.answerShort: The model's echelon turret layout identifies the 1911 battlecruiser, so the heavy-cruiser label appears to be a museum error.

segments.title: A quiet submarine must blend into the ocean
segments.body: Natural-convection reactors can be quieter than pumped systems, yet a nuclear submarine still produces some sound. The aim is to sink that signature into the irregular acoustic background of the ocean. A perfectly silent patch is compared to pure black standing out against a dark but textured night. Regular mechanical rhythms are especially revealing because natural sound rarely repeats on the same short cycle. Effective concealment therefore means sounding like the environment, perhaps even like marine life. That resemblance does not guarantee safety in wartime: the discussion cites fish and whales being depth-charged during the Falklands War as examples of mistaken contacts.

evidence.note: Natural convection, residual reactor noise, and the difficulty of concealing regular mechanical patterns in ocean sound.
The comparison with visual camouflage leads to marine-life masking and the caveat that fish and whales were attacked during the Falklands War.

segments.summary: Submarine stealth depends on blending with irregular ocean noise, since perfect silence or a repeating mechanical rhythm can reveal the boat.

segments.title: Limits of closer German-Japanese naval cooperation
segments.body: Germany and Japan already cooperated, so the counterfactual requires a deeper exchange of designs and industrial knowledge. segments.body: Modern submarines are designed to disappear into the acoustic background of the sea. segments.title: VLF and ELF links for submerged submarines
segments.body: Communicating with a submerged submarine is a harder problem than controlling an aircraft or surface vessel. Very-low-frequency transmissions reach submarines but have limited penetration and bandwidth. The VLF operators named in the discussion are Norway, France, the United States, Russia, Britain, Germany, Australia, Pakistan, and India. Extremely-low-frequency systems can reach operating depths of hundreds of metres, yet their antennas are enormous and depend on suitable geology. Only a small group of states has built such infrastructure, and some systems are uncertain or no longer active. Their data rates are measured in bits per second and messages often require error correction. Britain has VLF infrastructure rather than ELF; the frequencies given here are 3 to 30 kHz for VLF and 3 to 300 Hz for ELF. These links can tell a submarine to rise to a depth where it can receive a richer transmission, but they cannot provide continuous high-bandwidth remote control. The same constraint sharply limits concepts for globally operated uncrewed underwater vehicles.
